pages.x: When the Qin dynasty fell, one of its generals, Zhao Tuo, made himself king of Nanyue, the Southern Yue, with its capital at Panyu, today's Guangzhou. His kingdom reached into what is now northern Vietnam. For almost a century its kings honoured the Han emperors when it suited them, and called themselves emperors at home.

Emperor Wu of Han, who reigned for 54 years, pushed China's borders outward on every side. In 112 BC a minister of Nanyue, Lü Jia, killed the young king, his Chinese-born mother, who wanted to submit to the Han, and the Han envoys. Wu sent his armies south over the mountain passes and down the rivers.

In 111 BC one Han general reached Panyu first and set it on fire, and its defenders surrendered to another. Lü Jia and the new king fled by sea, and were caught. Nanyue was cut into nine commanderies reaching down to the Red River delta of Vietnam, and the next year the Han took Minyue, on the coast to the north, as well.

Northern Vietnam stayed under Chinese rule for about a thousand years, with many risings, the most famous led in AD 40 by two sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị, who are national heroines in Vietnam today. Vietnam won lasting independence only in 938.

Then Wu turned north-east, to Gojoseon, the oldest Korean kingdom, whose king, Ugeo, blocked the way to the lands beyond. In 109 BC one Han army crossed the Bohai Sea by ship while another marched overland. Both were beaten back at first, then closed in on the capital, Wanggeom, near today's Pyongyang.

In the summer of 108 BC, besieged and divided, Gojoseon's ministers murdered their king, and the capital fell. The Han split the land into four commanderies. The greatest, Lelang, around Pyongyang, lasted four centuries, and carried Chinese writing, tools and ideas into Korea and on to Japan.

The wars set the edges of the Chinese world for centuries. In Vietnam and Korea, Chinese writing, Confucian learning and later Buddhism took root, but both peoples kept their own languages, and fought long and proudly to rule themselves.
pts: Northern Vietnam was ruled from China for a thousand years
